Categorical summary table

Source: R/table_categorical.R
table_categorical.Rd

Builds a publication-ready frequency or cross-tabulation table for one or many categorical variables selected with tidyselect syntax.

With by, produces grouped cross-tabulation summaries (using cross_tab() internally) with a p-value per variable, from Pearson's chi-squared test or Fisher's exact test (see test), and optional association measures. Without by, produces one-way frequency-style summaries.

Multiple output formats are available via output: a printed ASCII table ("default"), a numeric data.frame ("data.frame", the displayed table, or "long", one row per variable, level and group), or publication-ready tables ("tinytable", "gt", "flextable", "excel", "clipboard", "word").

Usage

table_categorical(
  data,
  select = tidyselect::everything(),
  by = NULL,
  labels = getOption("spicy.var_labels", FALSE),
  levels_keep = NULL,
  include_total = TRUE,
  drop_na = FALSE,
  weights = NULL,
  rescale = getOption("spicy.rescale", FALSE),
  correct = FALSE,
  simulate_p = FALSE,
  simulate_B = 2000,
  test = c("auto", "chisq", "fisher", "midp", "n1"),
  p_value = NULL,
  p_adjust = "none",
  percent_digits = 1,
  p_digits = 3,
  effect_size_digits = 2,
  assoc_measure = "auto",
  assoc_ci = FALSE,
  smd = FALSE,
  decimal_mark = ".",
  align = c("decimal", "center", "right"),
  output = c("default", "data.frame", "long", "tinytable", "gt", "flextable", "excel",
    "clipboard", "word"),
  indent_text = "  ",
  indent_text_excel_clipboard = strrep(" ", 6),
  add_multilevel_header = TRUE,
  blank_na_wide = FALSE,
  excel_path = NULL,
  excel_sheet = NULL,
  clipboard_delim = "\t",
  word_path = NULL,
  user_na = TRUE,
  style = NULL,
  v_digits
)

Arguments

data

A data frame.

select

Columns to include as row variables. Supports tidyselect syntax and character vectors of column names. When omitted, defaults to every eligible categorical column in data: factor, character, logical, and labelled (haven / labelled) columns, excluding the by column – matching the select-less defaults of table_continuous() and table_continuous_lm(). An explicit select is taken verbatim (numeric columns included), so numeric-coded categorical variables can still be tabulated by naming them. The by and weights columns are not part of the selection: everything() and the other helpers skip them, and naming one in select, or giving its position, is an error. A name that is not a column of data is an error (class spicy_missing_column), and so is a selection with no column to tabulate. The levels of a variable are its rows in the order by gives its groups (see by); a labelled variable keeps the order of its codes.

by

Optional grouping column used for columns/groups. Accepts an unquoted column name or a single character column name. Factor levels keep their declared order, which is the way to choose another order; any other by is sorted, as in freq() and cross_tab(): text in the C locale (capitals before lower case, the same on every machine), FALSE before TRUE, numbers and the codes of a haven labelled column ascending, whatever the order of the rows. The column of missing values comes last. For a haven labelled by, the group headers are the raw codes (value labels are not used for group headers – the family convention shared with table_continuous() and table_continuous_lm()); declared missing values follow user_na as usual.

labels

How each variable is named in the table: in the rows, in the title, and in the notes. Four forms:

  • labels = FALSE shows the column name.

  • labels = TRUE shows the column's label attribute (as set by haven, labelled, or label_from_names()) when it is present, not NA, and not empty, and the column name otherwise.

  • labels = c(bmi = "Body mass index"), a named character vector, gives the columns it names these labels. Every other column follows options(spicy.var_labels): its name when the option is unset or FALSE, its label attribute when it is TRUE.

  • labels = var_labels(bmi = "BMI (kg/m2)") gives the columns it names these labels, and every other column its label attribute, whatever the option says. var_labels() alone is labels = TRUE.

Names that match no column are ignored, so one vector can serve every table of a project. The default reads options(spicy.var_labels), and a TRUE or FALSE typed in the call wins over it. Any other value, NULL included, is an error. A variable label documents the data file; a published table carries the wording you set here.

levels_keep

Levels to keep, in the order to display them. If NULL (the default), all observed levels are kept. Entries must match the level strings the table displays (for labelled columns these are the "[code] label" strings, not the bare label text). Two forms, as in table_categorical_svy():

  • a character vector applies to every variable: each keeps the levels it has, and a variable with none of them is dropped from the table with a classed warning (spicy_no_selection) listing its level strings;

  • a named list applies per variable (levels_keep = list(smoking = "Yes")): each name must be a variable of the table, each level one the variable displays (an error otherwise), and the variables it does not name keep all their levels.

include_total

Logical. If TRUE (the default), includes a Total group when available. A level of by displayed with the label of that margin is then an error (class spicy_label_collision): rename the level, or give the margin another label with options(spicy.labels = list(header_margin_total = "All")).

drop_na

Logical. The rule of the family: a table that counts shows the missing values by default, as a frequency table reports how many answers are missing; a table that computes a statistic removes them by default and counts them in the note (see table_continuous()). This table counts, so FALSE (the default) displays the missing values as a dedicated "(Missing)" level (and, under by, a "(Missing)" group column) – the field convention for descriptive tables (gtsummary's "Unknown" row, janitor's NA row; see the Epidemiologist R Handbook, Descriptive tables). A level displayed beside that row or column with its label is an error (class spicy_label_collision): rename the level, or give the row another label with options(spicy.labels = list(row_missing_level = "(Not stated)")). If TRUE, rows with NA in the tabulated variable (and in by, when supplied) are removed BEFORE each cross-tabulation, and the removal is disclosed in a table note ("Missing values removed: ...") rather than silent; a by that no observation holds is then an error (class spicy_invalid_data).

weights

Optional weights. Either NULL (the default), a numeric vector of length nrow(data), or a single column in data supplied as an unquoted name or a character string.

rescale

Logical. If FALSE, weights are used as-is. If TRUE, rescales weights so total weighted N matches raw N. Passed to spicy::cross_tab(). The default reads options(spicy.rescale), FALSE when it is unset, matching cross_tab().

correct

Logical. If FALSE (the default), no continuity correction is applied. If TRUE, applies Yates correction in 2x2 chi-squared contexts. Passed to spicy::cross_tab(). A variable tested by Fisher's exact test, its mid-p version, or the N-1 chi-squared (see test) takes no correction.

simulate_p

Logical. If FALSE (the default), uses asymptotic p-values. If TRUE, uses Monte Carlo simulation. Passed to spicy::cross_tab(). Applies to the Pearson chi-squared test only (see test).

simulate_B

Integer. Number of Monte Carlo replicates when simulate_p = TRUE, and for the Monte Carlo version of Fisher's exact test (see test). Defaults to 2000.

test

Character. The test of each variable when by is used. One of "auto" (default), "chisq", "fisher", "midp", or "n1".

  • "auto": Pearson's chi-squared test when every expected count of the variable's table is at least 5, Fisher's exact test otherwise, the rule of gtsummary's add_p(). The choice is made per variable, and the note names the test of each.

  • "chisq": Pearson's chi-squared test for every variable, the behavior before 0.14.0.

  • "fisher": Fisher's exact test for every variable.

  • "midp": the Fisher mid-p test for a 2x2 table.

  • "n1": the N-1 chi-squared test for a 2x2 table whose expected counts are all at least 1, Fisher's exact test for one with a smaller count (Campbell's rule).

Under "midp" and "n1", a variable whose table is not 2x2 follows "auto". correct and simulate_p apply to the Pearson chi-squared test only. When the exact enumeration of a large sparse table fails, Fisher's p-value is its Monte Carlo estimate over simulate_B tables, and the note says so; call set.seed() first to reproduce it. See Tests. Ignored when by is not used or when p_value = FALSE.

p_value

Logical or NULL. If TRUE and by is used, adds the p-value column of the test chosen by test. When NULL (the default), the p-value is shown automatically whenever by is supplied, and hidden otherwise. Pass p_value = FALSE to remove the test from every output: the p column, and the test_type, statistic, df and p.value columns of "long"; test, correct and simulate_p are then ignored, with a warning. The association measure keeps its own switch, so p_value = FALSE, assoc_measure = "none" gives a purely descriptive table. Ignored when by is not used.

p_adjust

Multiple-comparison adjustment of the p column, applied to the family of every test in the table (one p-value per variable). One of "none" (default), "holm", "hochberg", "hommel", "bonferroni", "BH" / "fdr", or "BY", as in table_regression(); delegated to stats::p.adjust(). Needs by and the p column. See Multiple-comparison adjustment.

percent_digits

Number of digits for percentages in report outputs. Defaults to 1. A whole number: a fraction is an error, as for every *_digits argument.

p_digits

Integer >= 1. Number of decimal places used to render p-values in the p column (default: 3, the APA Publication Manual standard). Both the displayed precision and the small-p threshold derive from this argument: p_digits = 3 prints .045 and <.001; p_digits = 4 prints .0451 and <.0001. Leading zeros are always stripped, following APA convention.

effect_size_digits

Number of digits for the association measure, its confidence interval and the SMD, as for the effect sizes of the other table functions. Defaults to 2.

assoc_measure

Which association measure to report alongside the p-value. Accepts four input shapes:

  • "none" – drop the column entirely.

  • "auto" (the default) – pick a measure per row variable based on the variable type: a 2x2 table (binary row variable vs. binary by) uses phi, a pair of ordered factors uses tau_b, every other case uses cramer_v.

  • a single string from c("cramer_v", "phi", "gamma", "tau_b", "tau_c", "somers_d", "lambda") – applied uniformly to every row variable.

  • a character vector with one entry per row variable. Both named (c(smoking = "phi", health = "tau_b"), recommended; unnamed variables fall back to "auto") and unnamed positional (c("phi", "tau_b", "auto"), paired up with select) are accepted. Named is more robust to reordering of select.

When a single measure is used for every row, the column header is that measure's name (e.g. "Cramer's V"). When multiple measures are used (typically with "auto" on a heterogeneous select), the header collapses to "Effect size" and the table note names the measure used for each variable.

phi requires a 2x2 table; if explicitly requested for a non-2x2 variable, an error is raised so the user can choose another measure or fall back to "auto".

assoc_ci

Passed to cross_tab(). If TRUE, includes the 95\ and in the "data.frame", "excel" and "clipboard" outputs, two extra columns headed 95\% CI LL / 95\% CI UL are added, the level stated as the other tables state it; in the long output ("long") the bounds fill es_ci_lower / es_ci_upper. In rendered formats ("gt", "tinytable", "flextable", "word"), the CI is shown inline (e.g., .14 [.08, .19]) under a header that states its level (Cramer's V [95\% CI]). Defaults to FALSE.

smd

Logical. If TRUE, adds an SMD column holding the standardized mean difference between the two groups of by, the balance diagnostic of the Table 1 literature. Requires exactly two groups; the value sits on the variable row beside p, never on a level row. Signed for a two-category variable (group 1 minus group 2 on the second category), unsigned for three or more, where it is a distance. No confidence interval and no p-value, by design. Rounded with effect_size_digits. See the "Standardized mean difference" section below. Defaults to FALSE.

decimal_mark

The decimal mark, a single character: "." (the default) or "," in most styles; the Lancet style of spicy_style() uses the middle dot.

align

Horizontal alignment of numeric columns in the printed ASCII table and in the tinytable, gt, flextable, word, and clipboard outputs. The first column (Variable) is always left-aligned. One of:

  • "decimal" (default): align numeric columns on the decimal mark, the standard scientific-publication convention used by SPSS, SAS, and LaTeX siunitx. Numeric cells are pre-padded with figure-spaces (U+2007, digit-width) so every string in a column has the same width with the decimal mark at the same internal position; centering those uniform-width strings then stacks the decimal points vertically. The same pad-then-center strategy is applied on every rendering engine (gt, tinytable, flextable, word, ASCII print) for a homogeneous rendering, matching table_regression() and table_continuous_lm(). The clipboard output is delimited text meant to be parsed rather than read at a fixed width, so its cells travel unpadded (a padded number pastes as text next to an unpadded number).

  • "center": center-align all numeric columns.

  • "right": right-align all numeric columns.

In the excel output, "center" centers the numeric columns and "right" is the same rendering as the default: cell-string padding does not align decimals under a proportional font, so "decimal" right-aligns instead, which combined with the per-column numfmt already produces dot-aligned columns. Same default and same three values as table_continuous() / table_continuous_lm(), whose workbooks resolve "decimal" differently: table_continuous() right-aligns only the counts and the p-value there, and table_continuous_lm() applies that convention at every align.

output

Output format. One of:

  • "default" (an ASCII table object, printed when the call is bare)

  • "data.frame" (the displayed table, numeric)

  • "long" (a long numeric data.frame)

  • "tinytable" (requires tinytable)

  • "gt" (requires gt)

  • "flextable" (requires flextable)

  • "excel" (requires openxlsx2)

  • "clipboard" (requires clipr)

  • "word" (requires flextable and officer)

indent_text

Prefix used for modality labels in report table building. Defaults to " " (two spaces).

indent_text_excel_clipboard

Stronger indentation used in Excel and clipboard exports. Defaults to six non-breaking spaces.

add_multilevel_header

Logical. If TRUE (the default), merges top headers in Excel export. Only consulted for output = "excel" on a grouped table (by supplied): typed with another output, it is ignored with a warning (class spicy_ignored_arg), like the other arguments of one output (excel_path, excel_sheet, clipboard_delim, word_path, ...), and a one-way table, which has a single header row to begin with, does not use it.

blank_na_wide

Logical. If FALSE (the default), NA values are kept as-is in output = "data.frame". If TRUE, the empty cells of its statistic columns become empty strings (the columns become text).

excel_path

Path for output = "excel", ending in ".xlsx", in a directory that exists. Defaults to NULL.

excel_sheet

Sheet name for Excel export. NULL (the default) uses "Categorical".

clipboard_delim

Delimiter for clipboard text export. Defaults to "\t". A cell holding the delimiter itself, a double quote or a line break is quoted RFC 4180-style, so the grid survives whatever delimiter you choose.

word_path

File path for output = "word", ending in ".docx", in a directory that exists. Defaults to NULL. Before 0.13.0, supplying it with output = "flextable" also wrote a .docx as a side effect; it is now used exclusively by output = "word" (the contract shared with the rest of the table family) and is ignored, with a warning, under any other output.

user_na

Logical. If TRUE (the default), declared missing values in the row variables and in by are treated as missing: they join the "(Missing)" level under drop_na = FALSE, and under drop_na = TRUE they are removed with a dedicated disclosure line (Declared missing values removed: ...). If FALSE, the declared codes stay valid categories. See the "Declared missing values" section of freq().

style

A journal style: a theme name ("jama", "nejm", "lancet", "annals", "apa", "aer"), a spicy_style() object, or NULL (the default). A style only changes DEFAULTS – any argument you pass explicitly wins over it. Set options(spicy.style = ) for document-wide scope. A theme covers numeric formatting conformity only, not full editorial conformity; ?spicy_style lists the exact rules each one encodes and the official document they come from. An unknown name is an error.

v_digits

Defunct. Renamed effect_size_digits in spicy 0.14.0, as in the other table functions; supplying v_digits is an error (class spicy_defunct).

Value

Depends on output:

  • "default": the underlying data.frame carrying the rendering metadata as attributes (S3 class "spicy_categorical_table"). The object is returned visibly, so a bare table_categorical(...) call auto-prints the styled ASCII table at the console while t <- table_categorical(...) stays silent (print t to display the table).

  • "data.frame": the displayed table with its numbers, what as.data.frame() of the default object returns: one row per printed row – the header row of each variable, which carries its p-value and its association measure, then one row per level. The key columns are variable (the column name), label (the label the rows display for it, see labels), level and .row_role ("factor_header", "level", or "missing" for the row of missing values the table adds), then the printed columns: one pair <group> n / <group> \% per group level (plus Total when include_total = TRUE), p (absent with p_value = FALSE), the association measure (named after the measure, or Effect size when the row variables do not share one), its bounds 95\% CI LL / 95\% CI UL with assoc_ci = TRUE, and SMD with smd = TRUE. When by = NULL, the printed columns are n and \%.

  • "long": a long data.frame, one row per variable, level and group, with columns variable, label, level, .row_role (the role of level: "level", or "missing" for the row of missing values), then, when by is used, group, .group_role (the role of group: "group", "missing" for the column of missing by values, or "total" for the margin) and total (TRUE on the rows of the margin), then n, pct (the percentage), then, with by, the test of the variable unless p_value = FALSE: test_type ("chi_squared" for Pearson's, "n1_chi_squared" for the N-1 chi-squared, "fisher_exact", "fisher_midp" for the Fisher mid-p test, or "fisher_exact_mc" for the Monte Carlo estimate of Fisher's exact test), statistic and df (the chi-squared, Pearson's or the N-1, NA for a variable tested by an exact test), p.value (and p_unadjusted under p_adjust); and the association measure, whichever measure it is: es_type names it per row ("cramer_v", "phi", ...), es_value holds it, es_ci_lower / es_ci_upper its interval (NA unless assoc_ci = TRUE), and smd_type ("binary" or "multinomial", the kernel the value came from) / smd_value the standardized mean difference. The measure and SMD columns are there whether or not they were requested, NA when not, so the schema does not move with an argument. The statistics of a variable sit on every row of its block.

  • "tinytable": a tinytable object.

  • "gt": a gt_tbl object.

  • "flextable": a flextable object.

  • "excel" / "word": writes to disk and returns the file path invisibly.

  • "clipboard": copies the table and returns the display data.frame invisibly.

The note, the drop_na = TRUE disclosure included, travels with the table on every route, not just the console: "default" prints it under the ASCII table, "tinytable" / "gt" / "flextable" / "word" carry it as a table note, "excel" writes it below the body, and the default object and the data frames of "data.frame" / "long" keep the whole note as printed, "Note." included, in attr(x, "note") (NULL when there is nothing to say), so a pipeline that renders the numbers itself can still state what left the table. On the "tinytable" route the note is set one size down; options(spicy.note_style) governs that (see table_regression()).

The Excel sheet carries the same title the console prints on its first row; the table itself starts on row 3.

Tests

When by is used, each selected variable is cross-tabulated against the grouping variable with cross_tab() and tested on the complete cases of its observed levels, a "(Missing)" level and a declared level nobody holds left out: one p-value per variable, in the p column. A table left with a single row or column (a variable observed at one level, or in one group) is uninformative and gets no test, whatever test says: its p cell shows a dash.

The chi-squared approximation is unreliable when expected counts are small. Under test = "auto", the default, a variable takes Pearson's chi-squared test (stats::chisq.test()) when every expected count of its table is at least 5, and Fisher's exact test (stats::fisher.test()) otherwise: the rule gtsummary's add_p() applies, with the same p-values. Fisher's exact test of a table larger than 2x2 is the Freeman-Halton extension. When its exact enumeration fails, which happens on large sparse tables, the p-value is its Monte Carlo estimate over simulate_B tables drawn with the observed margins: it is random, so call set.seed() first to reproduce it. test = "chisq" tests every variable by the chi-squared, the behavior before 0.14.0, and test = "fisher" every variable by the exact test.

Fisher's exact test is conservative: its actual level is often well below the nominal one, at a cost in power. test = "midp" gives a 2x2 table (a two-level variable by two groups) the Fisher mid-p test, as Fagerland, Lydersen and Laake (2017, equation 1.12, p. 28, and section 4.4.6, p. 97) and Lydersen, Fagerland and Laake (2009, equation 12, p. 1165) define it: the tables with the observed margins are ordered by their hypergeometric probability, and the p-value adds the probabilities of the tables less probable than the observed one to half the probabilities of the tables as probable, the observed one included, ties being read within the relative tolerance of stats::fisher.test(). The mid-p test can exceed the nominal level, usually by little, and Fagerland, Lydersen and Laake (2017, p. 175) recommend it for all sample sizes. A variable whose table is not 2x2 follows "auto", and the note names the test of each variable. The central variant, twice the smaller one-sided mid-p (the exact2x2 and epitools packages; Agresti, 2019, p. 49), coincides with this one when the row totals or the column totals are equal, except that it gives 1 for the most probable table; it differs otherwise and is not computed.

test = "n1" applies the rule of Campbell (2007, pp. 18-19) to a 2x2 table. When every expected count is at least 1, the table takes the N-1 chi-squared test: Pearson's statistic, with no continuity correction, multiplied by (N - 1)/N and referred to a chi-squared distribution with 1 degree of freedom, which is the Mantel-Haenszel statistic of a single 2x2 table; statistic and df hold that statistic in the long output. Otherwise it takes Fisher's exact test, two-sided by Irwin's rule as stats::fisher.test() computes it. Campbell found the N-1 test close to its nominal level under that restriction, not without it. A variable whose table is not 2x2 follows "auto", and the note names the test of each variable.

The note names the test of every variable, "Group comparison: Pearson chi-squared test (sex, education); Fisher exact test (smoking).", or the one test when it covers them all. test_type in the long output gives the same per variable. See @param correct / simulate_p to switch on Yates' continuity correction or Monte Carlo p-values for the chi-squared test, and @param assoc_measure for the per-row dispatch table used by "auto" (2x2 -> Phi, both ordered -> Kendall's Tau-b, otherwise Cramer's V). Without by, the table reports the marginal frequency distribution of each variable with no inferential statistics.

The exact tests condition on counts. Under weights, they run on the weighted table when its cells are whole numbers (frequency weights); otherwise a variable that a rule sends to Fisher's exact test keeps the chi-squared test, Pearson's under test = "auto" and the N-1 under Campbell's rule, with a warning (spicy_fallback), and test = "fisher", or test = "midp" on a 2x2 table, is an error. For survey weights, table_categorical_svy() gives the design-based test.

The test and the measure are two decisions with two arguments: p_value = FALSE removes the test, assoc_measure = "none" the measure. Together they give a purely descriptive table, which keeps the group columns and their headers; smd stays available.

For model-based comparisons (cluster-robust SE, weighted contrasts, fitted means) on continuous outcomes, see table_continuous_lm(). For descriptive (empirical) comparisons on continuous outcomes, see table_continuous().

Multiple-comparison adjustment

The p-values of a descriptive table describe: they test no prespecified hypothesis. STROBE (explanation of item 14) and the SAMPL guidelines advise against significance tests in descriptive and baseline tables, hence the default p_adjust = "none".

When a journal or a protocol asks for adjusted p-values anyway, p_adjust applies stats::p.adjust() to the family of every test in the table: one p-value per variable (one per block in table_outcome()), never the rows of one variable, which share one test. "holm" suits a confirmatory set of comparisons, "BH" a screening one; table_regression() lists the methods. A test that returned no p-value stays out of the family.

The adjustment runs before any formatting, so the p column and its <.001 threshold show the adjusted values, and the table note gives the number of tests and the method. The raw p-values stay in the object: a p_unadjusted column next to the p-value column of the returned data frames, and col_meta$p$p_unadjusted (with the method in p_adjust and the family size in p_adjust_m) in as_structured(). Without by, or with p_value = FALSE, the table shows no p-value to adjust, and a p_adjust other than "none" is an error.

Standardized mean difference

smd = TRUE adds an SMD column with the balance diagnostic of the Table 1 literature, on the variable row beside p. For a two-category variable it is the Bernoulli form,

$$\mathrm{SMD} = \frac{p_1 - p_2}{\sqrt{(p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2)) / 2}}$$

with \(p\) the proportion of the SECOND category, signed, group 1 minus group 2 in the order the table displays them. Note the denominator: the Bernoulli variance \(p(1-p)\) at n, not var() at \(n-1\), which would be 19% off on a small table.

"Second category" is the order the table shows, which is worth knowing for a logical variable: spicy displays TRUE then FALSE, so the sign is taken on FALSE, where tableone and cobalt coerce with factor() (FALSE, TRUE) and take it on TRUE – the same magnitude with the opposite sign. Convert to a factor with the level order you want if the direction matters.

For three or more categories it is the multivariate form of Yang and Dalton (2012, SAS Global Forum 335-2012),

$$\mathrm{SMD} = \sqrt{T' S^{-} T}$$

with \(T\) the difference of the two profiles of proportions (first category dropped) and \(S\) the mean of their multinomial covariance matrices. This is a Mahalanobis distance: it is unsigned, it is not bounded by 1, and \(S^{-}\) is a pseudo-inverse, because a declared-but-unobserved category makes \(S\) singular and solve() would abort where the pseudo-inverse returns exactly the value that category's absence implies. Which kernel a row took is published as smd_type in the "long" output, and the unsigned reading is stated in the table note whenever a variable has more than two categories. The MASS package is needed for this arm only.

Two profiles with no category in common have an infinite standardized distance. The pseudo-inverse would quietly publish a finite number there, so the cell is an en-dash and a classed warning says why. The same applies when each group is constant on a different category, where the naive route publishes 0 – "perfectly balanced" for the most imbalanced variable possible.

Conventions shared with table_continuous(): exactly two groups (three or more are refused, not averaged over pairs); complete cases on the observed groups, so a drop_na = FALSE "(Missing)" level is displayed and never enters the diagnostic; no confidence interval and no p-value, by design. Under weights the profiles are the weighted proportions, which makes this column agree with both the frequency and the survey-design readings – a profile of proportions is invariant to a global rescaling of the weights, so rescale cannot move it. (Only the continuous arm has a convention to choose there.)

The SMD cell keeps its leading zero where the association cell drops it: the APA strip belongs to a bounded measure, and this one is not bounded. The two columns therefore print 0.45 and .45 side by side, on purpose.

A balance table usually shows no test: p_value = FALSE removes the p column here as it does in table_continuous(), so a table mixing continuous and categorical variables can drop both. inline() quotes the cell from the variable row (inline(tbl, smoking, column = "smd")).

Display conventions

Decimal alignment, p-value formatting, and required suggested packages per output engine are documented under @param align, @param p_digits, and @param output respectively.

Counts are displayed as integers: weighted counts are rounded (ties half to even, the R convention) at display time only, in cells and margins alike – the SPSS Crosstabs convention. Cells and margins are rounded independently, so small display discrepancies are possible (e.g. two cells of exactly 0.5 each display as 0 while their Total of 1.0 displays as 1). The machine outputs ("data.frame", "long") carry the exact weighted counts and full-precision percentages.

Declared missing values

Survey files imported with haven often carry declared missing values: codes such as 8 = Don't know or 9 = Refused that the source file marks as missing while keeping them distinct from a plain NA. Two kinds of declaration exist: na_values / na_range metadata on haven::labelled_spss() vectors, and tagged missing values created by haven::tagged_na() (the Stata .a, .b, ... convention). haven::read_sav() keeps the na_values / na_range declaration only with user_na = TRUE: its default turns the declared codes into NA on import.

spicy honors the declaration by default (user_na = TRUE): declared missing values are excluded from every statistic exactly like NA – valid percentages, means, chi-squared tests, association measures, row-wise summaries, and group definitions – but they are not erased from display. freq() lists each observed declared value as its own row of the Missing block, with its value label; cross_tab(), table_categorical(), and table_continuous() disclose the exclusion in the table note (Declared missing values removed: x (2).); varlist() counts them as missing in N_valid / NAs / N_distinct while still listing the declared codes in Values; code_book() counts them in n_declared_missing and flags them in its values table.

Every function involved offers the same escape hatch: set user_na = FALSE to ignore the declaration and treat the declared codes as valid values (the behavior of spicy before 0.13.0). Tagged missing values are genuine NAs either way; for them, user_na = FALSE only collapses the per-tag breakdown back into the regular NA count.

References

Agresti, A. (2019). An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis (3rd ed.). Wiley.

Campbell, I. (2007). Chi-squared and Fisher-Irwin tests of two-by-two tables with small sample recommendations. Statistics in Medicine, 26(19), 3661-3675. doi:10.1002/sim.2832

Fagerland, M. W., Lydersen, S., & Laake, P. (2017). Statistical Analysis of Contingency Tables. Chapman and Hall/CRC. doi:10.1201/9781315374116

Lydersen, S., Fagerland, M. W., & Laake, P. (2009). Recommended tests for association in 2 x 2 tables. Statistics in Medicine, 28(7), 1159-1175. doi:10.1002/sim.3531

See also

table_continuous() for empirical comparisons on continuous outcomes; table_continuous_lm() for the model-based companion (heteroskedasticity-consistent / cluster-robust / bootstrap / jackknife SE, fitted means, weighted contrasts); cross_tab() for two-way cross-tabulations; freq() for one-way frequency tables.

Other spicy tables: table_continuous(), table_continuous_lm()

Examples

# --- Basic usage ---------------------------------------------------------

# Default: ASCII console table grouped by sex.
table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity),
  by = sex
)

# --- Per-variable association measure ----------------------------------

# Default (`assoc_measure = "auto"`): one measure per row variable based on
# the variable type (2x2 -> Phi, both ordered factors -> Kendall's Tau-b,
# otherwise Cramer's V). When the chosen measures differ across rows, the
# column header collapses to `"Effect size"` and the note names the
# measure used for each variable.
table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, education),
  by = sex
)

# The rendered outputs below all wrap the same call:
#   table_categorical(sochealth,

#                     by = sex)
# only `output` changes. Assign each result to a variable -- some
# engines auto-print as a console-friendly text fallback inside
# the `?` help viewer.

# Wide data.frame (one row per modality).
table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity),
  by = sex,
  output = "data.frame"
)

# \donttest{
# Rendered HTML / docx objects -- best viewed inside a
# Quarto / R Markdown document or a pkgdown article.
if (requireNamespace("tinytable", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tt <- table_categorical(
    sochealth, select = c(smoking, physical_activity), by = sex,
    output = "tinytable"
  )
}
if (requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tbl <- table_categorical(
    sochealth, select = c(smoking, physical_activity), by = sex,
    output = "gt"
  )
}
if (requireNamespace("flextable", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ft <- table_categorical(
    sochealth, select = c(smoking, physical_activity), by = sex,
    output = "flextable"
  )
}

# Excel and Word: write to a temporary file.
if (requireNamespace("openxlsx2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
  table_categorical(
    sochealth, select = c(smoking, physical_activity), by = sex,
    output = "excel", excel_path = tmp
  )
  unlink(tmp)
}
if (
  requireNamespace("flextable", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("officer", quietly = TRUE)
) {
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".docx")
  table_categorical(
    sochealth, select = c(smoking, physical_activity), by = sex,
    output = "word", word_path = tmp
  )
  unlink(tmp)
}

)
